lesson.title: Everything Else: The Power of the Complement
lesson.summary: The complement rule, P(not A) = 1 minus P(A), turns miserable at least one problems into a single easy subtraction by computing the opposite event instead.
lesson.body:
The complement of an event A, written A complement, is every outcome in the sample space that is not in A. Every outcome belongs to exactly one of the two groups, either inside A or outside it, never both and never neither, which means A and its complement always split the entire sample space into two non overlapping pieces. Because A and its complement are disjoint and together cover all of S, the addition rule from the previous chapters says P(A) plus P(A complement) must equal P(S), which equals 1. Rearranging that single equation gives the complement rule: P(A complement) = 1 minus P(A). The complement rule is not a separate law of probability handed down from nowhere, it falls directly out of the addition rule applied to the simplest possible pair of disjoint events, an event and everything that is not that event.

The complement rule earns its own chapter because it solves a specific, recurring headache: some events are miserable to compute directly but trivial to compute through their opposite. This shows up constantly in at least one problems, questions that ask for the probability that something happens at least once across several repeated trials. Computed directly, an at least one question forces you to add up the probability of exactly one success, exactly two successes, exactly three successes, and so on, tracking every way the event could partially or fully occur without double counting any of them. Computed through the complement, the same question collapses into a single easy case: the probability that the event never happens at all.

Consider rolling two fair, independent dice and asking for the probability of rolling at least one six. Attacking this directly means separately counting rolls with a six on the first die only, a six on the second die only, and six on both, then carefully adding those three disjoint pieces without double counting the outcome where both dice show six. It is doable, but easy to get wrong.

The complement approach is cleaner. The complement of at least one six is no six on either die. Since the two dice do not influence each other, the probability neither die shows a six is the probability the first die avoids six, five out of six, combined with the probability the second die also avoids six, another five out of six, a reasoning the multiplication rule chapter ahead will formalize fully. That gives P(no six on either die) = 5/6 times 5/6 = 25/36. Applying the complement rule, P(at least one six) = 1 minus 25/36, which equals 11/36. That single subtraction replaces the entire messy three case computation from the direct approach, and it agrees with it exactly.

Notice that A and its complement are themselves the simplest possible example of two events that share no outcomes at all, disjoint by definition, since nothing can simultaneously happen and not happen on the same trial. The next chapter widens the lens from this one special pair to disjoint events in general, any two events that cannot occur together, whether or not one is literally the complement of the other.
